summary: Describes an EPP extension for provisioning and managing DNSSEC information for domain names stored in a shared registry. It extends the EPP domain name mapping, specified in XML, to carry the data needed for DNS security. It is a standards-track document that was later replaced by RFC 5910.

plainLanguage.summary: Registrars use a messaging system to update domain records. This extension lets them also hand over the security keys that protect the domain.

questions: how to provision dnssec in a registry
how to provision dnssec in registry
subtitle: Managing DNS security keys through the domain provisioning protocol.

tldr.problem: Registries needed a way for registrars to provision and manage DNSSEC delegation signer (DS) information for domains through the EPP protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4310 defines an XML extension to EPP that lets registrars supply DNSSEC delegation signer data, including key information and optional parameters, when creating or updating domains.
tldr.outcome: Registries can now automate the provisioning of DNSSEC protection for domains through the standard EPP channel, linking the domain registration process to DNS security.

today: RFC 4310 is a Proposed Standard that was later superseded by RFC 5910. The core concepts remain valid for EPP implementations that support DNSSEC provisioning through registries.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
RFC 4310 describes an extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), which registrars use to manage domains in a central registry. The extension is specifically designed to support the provisioning and management of Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) for domain names stored in a shared central repository.

The base EPP protocol is defined in RFC 3730, and RFC 3731 describes the EPP domain name mapping. This extension builds on that foundation, specified in XML, to carry the additional data required for DNS security. Understanding DNSSEC, as described in RFCs 4033, 4034, and 4035, is essential to grasp the security concepts discussed in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Registrars use EPP to talk to registries. This extension adds DNSSEC security information to what they can send.

sections.title: DNSSEC Delegation Signer Information
sections.content:
At the heart of this extension is the Delegation Signer (DS) record. A DS record is published by a parent DNS zone to indicate that a child zone is digitally signed and that the parent recognizes a particular key as valid for the child zone. According to RFC 4034, a DS record contains four fields: a key tag (a short numeric identifier for the key), a key algorithm number, an octet identifying the digest algorithm used, and a digest field (the cryptographic hash).

When a registrant wants to enable DNSSEC for their domain, the registry must publish DS records that reference the domain's signing keys. RFC 4310 allows registrars to supply this DS information through EPP, either by providing the digest directly or, optionally, by supplying the public key data itself so the registry can compute the digest. The extension also supports the optional maxSigLife parameter, which indicates how long signatures should remain valid.
sections.plainLanguage: A DS record is like a fingerprint of your domain's security key. It tells the parent zone how to check that your domain's security is real.

sections.title: EPP Command Mapping
sections.content:
The extension maps to five EPP operations: query commands (check, info, transfer) and transform commands (create, delete, renew, transfer, update). For query commands, only the info command response is extended; the client does not provide DNSSEC data in the request, but the response includes a <secDNS:infData> element containing the DS data currently associated with the domain, including any key tags, algorithms, digests, and optional maximum signature lifetime values.

For transform commands, the create command requires a <secDNS:create> element containing one or more DS data elements. The update command is the most flexible, providing three operations: <secDNS:add> to add new DS information, <secDNS:rem> to remove DS data by key tag, and <secDNS:chg> to replace all DS information with new data. An optional urgent attribute on the update element allows clients to request high-priority processing of security updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Registrars can ask the registry for a domain's current security info, or add, remove, or change the security keys.

sections.title: XML Schema and Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The extension is formally specified in XML Schema notation, defining the structure and validation rules for all DNSSEC extension elements. The schema defines complex types for DS data (dsDataType) containing fields for the key tag (an unsigned 16-bit integer), algorithm (an unsigned byte), digest type (an unsigned byte), and digest (a hexadecimal binary field). Optional fields include maxSigLife (a positive integer representing seconds) and keyData elements containing the public key information.

Public key data, when supplied, follows the DNSKEY record format from RFC 4034, with fields for flags, protocol, algorithm, and the encoded public key. All elements are validated against this schema, ensuring that EPP clients and servers can reliably exchange DNSSEC information without ambiguity or syntax errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines exactly how the security data should be written in XML so computers can check that it is correct.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that key data provided by the client is optional; the server is not obligated to use it. Server operators may issue out-of-band DNS queries to retrieve key data from the domain's DNS apex to validate the DS information independently. It is recommended that domain operators publish their DNSKEY records in the DNS tree so that parent zone administrators can validate the DS data as necessary.

The RFC specifies that the Secure Entry Point (SEP) bit, as described in RFC 3757, SHOULD be set on key data when supplied. Additionally, internationalization considerations follow standard EPP practices, and formal IANA considerations apply to the XML namespace registration for the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Registries can check the security keys by looking them up in DNS. Domain owners should publish their real keys online so the registry can verify them.
